papers.title_in_file: Photon Conversion in Thin-film Lithium Niobate Nanowaveguides: A Noise Analysis
papers.version_note: arXiv:2102.07044v1 (14 Feb 2021); the header carries a compile date of November 27, 2024.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental noise analysis of telecom to 775 nm sum frequency conversion with a small detuned telecom pump in an 8 mm periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate nanowaveguide, attributing noise to Raman scattering and SPDC after residual second harmonic generation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the device is an 8 mm long PPLN nanowaveguide on a 500 nm thick, X cut, magnesium doped lithium niobate thin film bonded on silicon dioxide on a silicon base, with a top width of 1.8 µm, a poling period of 2.5 µm, and a chip temperature stabilized at 48±0.1 degree.
quotes: an 8-mm long PPLN nanowaveguide is fabricated on a 500 nm thick, X-cut, magnesiumdoped lithium niobate thin film bonded on silicon dioxide
The top width is measured to be 1.8 µm.
The nanowaveguide is periodically poled with a period of 2.5 µm to compensate for phase mismatching.
The chip is placed on a stage whose temperature is stabilized at 48±0.1 degree.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report a highest internal conversion efficiency of 65% when the pump power on chip is 430 mW, limited by propagation loss, and state that the conversion efficiency would have been 99.9% if there were no waveguide loss.
quotes: the highest internal conversion efficiency is 65% when the pump power on chip is 430 mW
the conversion efficiency would have been 99.9% if there were no waveguide loss
assertions.reader_inference: The 99.9% figure is a calculation with the loss set to zero, not a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors report a normalized efficiency ηnor=863% W −1cm−2 for the nanowaveguide, which they attribute to the tight mode confinement and the large nonlinear susceptibility d33 of lithium niobate.
quotes: the normalized efficiency is ηnor=863% W −1cm−2, thanks to the tight mode confinement and lithium niobate’s largest nonlinear susceptibility d33

assertions.value: The authors fit the measured internal conversion efficiency η to ηmax times a sine squared function of an argument built from ηnor, P and L (the text layer prints the equation without its radical sign), where ηmax is the maximum conversion efficiency limited by the propagation loss, P is the pump peak power on chip and L is the waveguide length.
quotes: η = ηmaxsin2( ηnorP L).
ηmax is the maximum conversion efficiency limited by the propagation loss, P is the pump peak power on chip, and L denotes the nnaowaveguide length.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II defines each symbol of the fit model it uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the conversion sweep the signal was fixed at the peak sum frequency generation wavelength and a power of 214 µW while the pump power was increased from 62 mW to 1230 mW.
quotes: a power of 214 µW, while the pump power is gradually increased from 62 mW to 1230 mW.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pump is created by carving the output of a 1559.7 nm continuous-wave laser into a 10 MHz, 10 ns pulse train by an electro-optical modulator, and that at high pump power the signal wavelength is tuned slightly around 1540.5 nm to compensate for the thermal effect.
quotes: The pump is created by carving the output of a 1559.7 nm continuous-wave laser into a 10 MHz, 10 ns pulse train by an electro-optical modulator.
the signal wavelength is tuned slightly around 1540.5 nm to compensate for the thermal effect
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the up-converted signal at 775 nm and the remaining noise are recorded by a visible single-photon detector (ID100) with a detection efficiency of 15%, that two band-pass filters with a 3 nm bandwidth reject the residual second-harmonic light at 779.9 nm by over 120 dB, and that telecom-band photons are recorded by a four-channel SNSPD with a detection efficiency around 85%.
quotes: Then the up-converted signal at 775 nm and the remaining noise are recorded by a visible single-photon detector (ID100), with a detection efficiency of 15%.
The SF light is further cleaned by two band-pass filters with a 3-nm bandwidth to reject the residual SH light at 779.9 nm by over 120 dB.
whose detection efficiency is around 85%
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that they did not measure noise directly at the 1540.5 nm signal wavelength, to avoid potential underestimation of the noise counts, and instead set two tunable filters at 1551.7 nm and 1567.7 nm, on the two sides of the pump and outside the up-conversion window.
quotes: we don't directly measure noise at signal wavelength 1540.5 nm directly to avoid potential underestimation of the noise counts [7].
the wavelength of those two tunable filters are set to be 1551.7nm and 1567.7nm, respectively, symmetrically residing at two sides of the pump and both out of the upconversion window.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A states the measurement design and so the wavelengths at which the signal-band noise was actually counted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the total coupling loss from the nanowaveguide input to the SNSPD input fiber is 20.9 dB at 1551.7 nm and 19.4 dB at 1567.7 nm, that the input coupling loss of the nanowaveguide is estimated at 4 dB for both wavelengths from a similar waveguide, and that the transmission from the nanowaveguide to the detectors is η1=1.74% and η2=2.45% for the two wavelengths.
quotes: The total coupling loss from the input of the nanowaveguide to the input fiber of the SNSPD are 20.9 dB for 1551.7 nm and 19.4 dB for 1567.7 nm, respectively.
The input coupling loss of the nanowaveguide is estimated to be 4 dB for both wavelengths
η1=1.74% and η2=2.45% for the two wavelengths
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that there are four possible mechanisms for background photons at the signal wavelength: SHG-SPDC noise, spontaneous Raman scattering in the input fiber, spontaneous Raman scattering in the nanowaveguide, and spontaneous four-wave mixing.
quotes: There are four possible mechanisms to create background photons at the signal wavelength: the SHGSPDC noise, SRS in both the input fiber and the nanowaveguide, and noise through spontaneous fourwave mixing (SFWM).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A states the set of noise mechanisms its analysis covers.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the pump is on the Stokes side of the signal, no SPDC noise is generated directly by the pump.
quotes: As the pump is on the Stokes side of the signal, there is no SPDC noise generated directly by the pump.

assertions.value: The authors state that SHG-SPDC and spontaneous four-wave mixing both occur at a rate quadratic to the applied pump power, and report that the on-chip photon pair generation rate is fitted well with a quadratic function.
quotes: Thus both occur at a rate quadratic to the applied pump power.
the PPG rate is fitted well with a quadratic function

assertions.value: The authors report that the total signal-band noise increases nearly linearly with low pump power but shows a quadratic dependency at high pump power.
quotes: the total noise increases nearly linearly with low pump power, but showing a quadratic dependency for high pump power.

assertions.value: The authors report that at a pump power of approximately 200 mW, corresponding to an internal up-conversion efficiency close to 50%, the photon pair generation noise accounts for 42% of the total noise.
quotes: for pump power ∼200 mW, corresponding to an internal up-conversion efficiency close to 50%, the PPG noise accounts for 42% of the total noise.
assertions.reader_inference: The 200 mW operating point is stated with a flat gain assumption over 11 nm; see the assumption entry.

assertions.value: The authors state that they assume a flat SPDC gain spectrum over an 11 nm bandwidth from 1551.7 nm to 1540.5 nm, citing it as typical, and that their Eq. (3) is valid only when photon pair generation dominates other noise sources.
quotes: we have assumed a flat SPDC gain spectrum over a bandwidth of 11 nm, from 1551.7 nm to 1540.5 nm, which is typically the case [23, 24].
Also, Eq. (3) is valid only when PPG dominates other noise sources.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A states the assumption and the validity condition of its own estimate.

assertions.value: The authors report that the coincidence to accidental ratio drops from 147 to 35 as the pump power increases, and conclude that the coincident counts mostly come from photon pair generation.
quotes: CAR drops from 147 to 35, which nonetheless remains significantly higher than 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that an unpoled nanowaveguide of similar geometry, with a 100 nm wider top, on the same chip gave a coincidence to accidental ratio of 1 even at the highest EDFA pump power, which they state rules out spontaneous four-wave mixing as a contributor to the photon pair generation.
quotes: another nanowaveguide without poling, of the similar geometry but with a 100 nm wider top, is fabricated on the same chip.
Even at the highest power setting of the EDFA for the pump, the CAR turns out to be 1.
This result rules out SFWM’s contribution to the PPG.

assertions.value: The authors describe the SHG-SPDC noise as a cascaded second-order process in which two pump photons merge into a visible photon that spontaneously down-converts into a pair of nondegenerate photons over a broad spectrum, and spontaneous four-wave mixing as direct photon pair generation from the pump through the Kerr nonlinearity.
quotes: The first involves a cascaded χ(2) process, where two pump photons merge into a visible photon that spontaneously down-converts a pair of nondegenerate photons over a broad spectrum.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A defines the two photon pair mechanisms the analysis separates.

assertions.value: The authors report that spontaneous Raman scattering in the input fiber takes up around 30% of the total noise when the internal conversion efficiency is less than 40%, and state that it can be reduced with a shorter input fiber; the input fiber is four meters long.
quotes: the in-fiber Raman noise takes up a significant part of the total noise, around 30% when the internal conversion efficiency is less than 40%.
SFWM noise created in the four-meter input fiber is negligible [22].
assertions.reader_inference: The four-meter length is quoted from a sentence about four-wave mixing in the same fiber.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Raman noise created in the nanowaveguide, obtained by subtraction, depends linearly on pump power, leads before the on-chip pump power reaches 125 mW, and that above that power the SPDC noise becomes the main source because of its quadratic dependence on pump power.
quotes: which exhibits a good linear dependence on the pump power, as expected. It takes the lead before the on chip pump power reaches 125 mW.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Raman noise rate measured with constant second-harmonic power across the waveguide overestimates the direct SRS level, and derive that for the same second-harmonic power at the output the noise rate in the up-conversion case is Rt = Rv/3.
quotes: Note that this is an overestimate of the direct SRS level.
Therefore, for the same SH power at the output, Rt = Rv/3,
assertions.reader_inference: The factor of one third follows from the authors' assumption that the second harmonic grows quadratically along an undepleted pump.

assertions.value: The authors report that the direct spontaneous Raman scattering of the residual second harmonic contributes at most 11% of the total noise in the sum frequency band.
quotes: the direct SRS followed by the residual SHG contributes at most 11% of the total noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that the indirect SRS noise, in which the pump is first Raman scattered into the signal band and then up-converted, adds significantly to the total noise in the sum frequency band.
quotes: From the above measurement results, the indirect SRS noise
adds significantly to the total noise in the SF band.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Raman spectrum was measured with a 10 MHz, 10 ns pulse train prepared at 1537.5 nm as pump, and that photon counts were taken as the tunable filters were swept from 1550 nm to 1605 nm in 1 nm steps.
quotes: a pulse train with 10 MHz repetition rate and 10 ns pulse width is prepared at 1537.5nm, to use as the pump.
Photon counts are taken as the tunable filters are swept from 1550 nm to 1605 nm at step size of 1 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.C states the setup of the spectrum measurement.

assertions.value: The authors report an obvious Raman peak at 254/cm on the Stokes side, which they state coincides with previous Raman spectrum studies of congruent lithium niobate.
quotes: An obvious peak is erected at 254/cm, which coincides the previous Raman spectrum study in congruent lithium niobate[4, 20].

assertions.value: The authors report that the measurement suggests a region free of Raman active peak, from 150/cm to 210/cm, for photon conversion by small-detuned pumping with relatively low noise.
quotes: The result also suggests a suitable region free of Raman active peak, from 150/cm to 210/cm, for photon conversion by small-detuned pumping with relative low noise.

assertions.value: The authors define a time-frequency mode as a minimum uncertainty mode with the least area in the time and frequency phase space, and state that the number of modes for each pump pulse is given by BT, with B the area subtended by the effective spectral filter profile and T the effective width of the time window.
quotes: a time-frequency mode is defined a minimum uncertainty mode with the least area in the time and frequency phase space
the number of time-frequency modes is given by BT
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III defines the unit in which all its noise figures are reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the signal-band noise, counted through a 0.6 nm filter, has B = 75 GHz and with T = 10 ns gives 750 detection modes, that the SHG-SRS measurement through a 3 nm filter gives 1.5 × 104 modes (exponent printed flat in the text layer, ten to the fourth), and that the sum frequency band is taken as B = 0.56 THz giving 5600 modes.
quotes: the noise photons in the signal band are counted after passing through a 0.6 nm filer, so that B = 75 GHz. With T = 10 ns, the number of detection modes is 750.
The SHG-SRS noise is measured with a 3 nm filter, so that the mode number is 1.5 × 104.
the detection mode number is calculated with B = 0.56 THz to be 5600.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the mode counting used to normalize its noise figures.

assertions.value: The authors state that the phase matching bandwidth of the PPLN nanowaveguide is only 4.5 nm in the telecom band, corresponding to 1.1 nm in the visible band, so only noise photons created within the 4.5 nm band around the signal wavelength can be up-converted to the sum frequency band.
quotes: the phase matching bandwidth of the PPLN nanowaveguide is only 4.5 nm in the telecom band, corresponding to 1.1 nm in the visible band.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the bandwidth that bounds which noise reaches the sum frequency band.

assertions.value: The authors report a total noise level of ∼ 10−4 per time-frequency mode in the sum frequency band when the internal conversion efficiency is about 49% (75% if there were no propagation loss).
assertions.anchor: Section I, p.2; Section III, p.5
quotes: Our result finds the total noise level to be ∼ 10−4 per time-frequency mode in the sum frequency (SF) band when the internal conversion efficiency is about 49% (75% if there were no propagation loss).
in the current configuration, the total noise created in the SF band is 10−4 per mode.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not state how many devices or repeat runs support this figure; Table I gives 9.96 for the same configuration.

assertions.value: In Table I, for the current experiment at 49% conversion (75% if no loss), the authors list 60.26 for in-waveguide SRS, 31.87 for in-fiber SRS and 54.00 for SHG-SPDC in the signal band, and 0.27 for SHG-SRS and 9.96 for the total in the sum frequency band, in units of 10−5 photons per detection mode.
quotes: Current Experiment, 49% Conversion (75% if no loss) 60.26 31.87 54.00 0.27 9.96
All numbers are given in 10−5 photons per detection mode.
assertions.reader_inference: Column attribution follows the heading order and band labels in the extracted text; the table layout itself was not seen.

assertions.value: In Table I the authors project the total sum frequency band noise, in units of 10−5 photons per detection mode, as 6.15 with the input fiber reduced to 1 m, 4.88 with the input fiber eliminated, 9.39 with residual SHG reduced by half, 8.81 with residual SHG eliminated, 5.57 with reduced input fiber and residual SHG, and 3.73 with no input fiber or residual SHG.
quotes: Input Fiber Reduced to 1 m 60.26 7.97 54.00 0.27 6.15
Input Fiber Eliminated 60.26 54.00 0.27 4.88
Residual SHG Reduced by Half 60.26 31.87 27.00 0.14 9.39
Residual SHG Eliminated 60.26 31.87 8.81
Reduced Input Fiber and Residual SHG 60.26 7.97 27.00 0.14 5.57
No Input Fiber or Residual SHG 60.26 3.73
All numbers are given in 10−5 photons per detection mode.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer drops standalone zero cells, so rows with zeros are quoted without them.

assertions.value: The authors state that reducing the input fiber to 1 meter and improving periodic poling to suppress residual SHG can lower the sum frequency band noise to 5.57 × 10−5, and that eliminating the input fiber and residual SHG entirely can lower it further to 3.73 × 10−5.
quotes: By reducing the input fiber to 1 meter and improving periodic poling to suppress residual SHG, it can be lowered to 5.57 × 10−5.
this noise can be further suppressed to 3.73 × 10−5 by totally eliminating the input fiber and residual SHG.
assertions.reader_inference: These are projections from the measured breakdown, not measurements of a modified device.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that, from analyzing the origins of the noise and its dependence on pump power and wavelength detuning, they identified a formula for noise suppression to 10−5 photons per mode.
quotes: we have also identified a formula for noise suppression to 10−5 photons per mode.
assertions.reader_inference: The body gives projected values of 5.57 and 3.73 in units of 10−5, not a measured value at 10−5 or below.

assertions.value: The authors state that the remaining and most critical noise source compromising single-photon conversion in PPLN nanowaveguides is the in-waveguide SRS that produces noise photons in the phase-matching bandwidth of the sum frequency generation.
quotes: Ultimately, the remaining yet most critical noise source compromising the single-photon conversion in PPLN nanowaveguides is the in-waveguide SRS that produces noise photon in the phase-matching bandwidth of SFG.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the limit its own noise breakdown leaves.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that SRS noise can be reduced by lowering the operating temperature of the PPLN nanowaveguides because Raman scattering depends on temperature, and propose designing the poling period for much lower temperature operation, which they say potentially leads to a several-fold decrease of intrinsic noise photons.
quotes: SRS noise can be reduced by lowering the operating temperature of the PPLN nanowaveguides[29] due to the temperature-dependent nature of Raman scattering [30].
potentially leads to several-fold decrease of intrinsic noise photon[29] after discounting the input fiber and residual SHG.
assertions.reader_inference: No low-temperature measurement is reported in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that by using a small detuned pump in the same telecom band the noise level may be acceptable for some quantum applications, and that spontaneous Raman scattering in the waveguide and SPDC following the residual SHG of the pump dominate among the noise sources.
quotes: our results reveal that, by using a small detuned pump in the same telecom band, the noise level may be acceptable for some quantum applications.
Among multiple noise sources, the spontaneous Raman scattering in the waveguide and SPDC following the residual SHG of the pump dominate.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Raman noise can be mitigated by parking the pump wavelength at the valley of the Raman gain spectrum and lowering the operating temperature, and that the residual SHG SPDC noise can be suppressed by improving the periodic poling quality.
quotes: The former can be mitigated by parking the pump wavelength at the valley of the Raman
The latter can be suppressed by reducing the residual SHG by, for example, improving the periodic poling quality.
assertions.reader_inference: The pump in the noise experiments was at 1559.7 nm; the valley placement was not tested in a conversion run.

assertions.value: The authors claim to report the first dedicated experimental characterization of the quantum noise and its attributions in a nanophotonic waveguide on thin-film lithium niobate.
quotes: We have reported the first dedicated experimental characterization of the quantum noise and its attributions in a nanophotonic waveguide on thin-film lithium niobate.

assertions.value: The authors state that in reverse proton exchange or ridge periodically poled lithium niobate devices there are two dominant noise processes detrimental to quantum frequency conversion, spontaneous Raman scattering and spontaneous parametric down conversion of the pump, citing earlier work.
quotes: there are two dominant noise processes detrimental to QFC: the spontaneous Raman scattering (SRS) and spontaneous parametric down conversion (SPDC) of the pump [4].

assertions.value: The authors state that for telecom-band quantum signals the pump wavelength must be in the vicinity of 2 microns to effectively eliminate broadband SPDC noise, which they say makes the conversion system costly, inconvenient or complicated.
quotes: Yet, for telecom-band quantum signals, their wavelength must be in the vicinity of 2 microns for effective elimination of broadband SPDC noise

assertions.value: The authors state two distinct factors that may significantly affect noise in thin-film lithium niobate waveguides compared with bulk counterparts: the crystalline structure is first destroyed and recovered during production, potentially altering the phonon modes, and significant pump mode leakage into the cladding layer.
quotes: First, during the production of TFLN, its crystalline structure is first destroyed and recovered, thus potentially altering the phonon modes [18].
Second, there is significant pump mode leakage into the cladding layer surrounding the PPLN nanowaveguide.

assertions.value: The authors state that with a small detuned telecom pump, in fiber optical networks the pump can be derived from the same master laser as the signal, allowing easy and jitter-free synchronization for the whole system.
quotes: in fiber optical networks such a pump can be derived from the same master laser as the signal, allowing easy and jitter-free synchronization for the whole system

assertions.value: The authors state that the total noise level is measured as a function of the applied pump power at a pulse repetition rate of 10 MHz, for conversion of the telecom C-band to the near visible regime around 780 nm in an X-cut PPLN nanowaveguide.
quotes: Here, we measure the total noise level as a function of the applied pump power, at a pulse repetition rate of 10 MHz.
we focus on QFC of telecom C-band to near visible regime around 780 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I states the scope of the measurements.
